title: Planning: Budget, Allocation, Roadmap, Objectives

know: Larson's planning as three separated discussions: the financial plan, functional allocation, and the roadmap.
How the vision-led roadmap of chapter 11 enters that process.
Team objectives as the contract, and OKRs as one form of them.
believe: Stable allocation lets teams commit; rebalancing every quarter destroys what was started.
Objectives are outcomes a team answers for, and a list of projects is not an objective.
can_do: Write a team objective and say what it is a contract for.
Shorten a planning cycle by removing what it should not be deciding.

audience.who: Executives (CEO, CTO, CPO, VP, Director) who run or sit in planning, and engineers, product managers and designers whose quarter is decided by it and who want to follow why it takes the form it does.
already_knows: How software teams work, and what annual and quarterly planning feel like from the inside.

From Part III: outcomes, the vision and the strategy steps, the roadmap with its three horizons, its share of capacity for innovation, iteration and operation, and the line between what leaders and teams decide.
From chapter 22: a decision right as a named decider, required advice and a record.
The book's failure-pattern names and Corvane's story up to 2026.
does_not_know: capacity (the book's sense: the working time of people in teams)
Larson's three cost segments (headcount, production, development)
allocation (of capacity to areas) and functional portfolio allocation (Larson's term)
OKR, key result, committed and aspirational objectives
operation share and learning cycle (each recalled in a clause)
Larson's four team states (recalled in a clause)

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a planning process, the reader identifies which of the three decisions are tangled and proposes the order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In a company's annual planning, each director presents a list of projects with headcount requests; the executive team ranks all projects in one spreadsheet and cuts from the bottom. Using only this chapter: what is tangled, and how would you run it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Budget, allocation and roadmap are decided at once at project level; first fix the financial envelope, then allocate capacity to areas (kept stable), then let each area choose outcomes and state them as team objectives; projects are the teams' business.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter states explicitly how Larson's capacity-first planning and Build What Matters' vision-first planning fit together, and where they would conflict.
OKR practice beyond the author's sources is credited to its source and marked as supplementing them.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

thesis.question: How do capacity planning and outcome planning fit into one process?
thesis.claim: Capacity planning and outcome planning fit into one process as successive decisions: first the financial plan fixes how much the organization can spend, then allocation assigns capacity to areas and holds it steady, then each area chooses the outcomes its capacity will pursue from the vision-led roadmap, and team objectives record that choice as a contract between leaders and teams — Larson's model answers how much goes where, Build What Matters answers what it is for, and they conflict only when one is asked to do the other's job.
thesis.disputed_by: Project-based planning, in which the unit of decision is a funded project with a business case, ranked against all other projects each cycle.
thesis.so_what: A leader stops ranking projects, keeps allocation stable across cycles, and reviews objectives by outcome.
thesis.how_why: Ranking projects decides budget, capacity and content at once, with the least information, and re-decides them every cycle. Separated, each decision is made by those who have its information — finance and executives, then area leaders, then teams — and only the last needs to change often.

supporting_claims.claim: Planning that negotiates budget, headcount, roadmap and team goals together makes three decisions at once with the least information, re-decides all of them every cycle, and takes longer with every person who must agree.

Planning is made of three decisions that differ in their question, in who holds the information and in how often they should change: the financial plan, the allocation of capacity to areas, and the choice of outcomes; made in that order, each fixes what the next works within.

The financial plan is fixed for the year and the allocation is held steady in large units and changed narrowly, because teams can commit to an outcome only if the capacity for it will still be there next quarter.

The vision-led roadmap enters at the third decision: each area chooses from it the outcomes its allocated capacity will pursue, and a team objective records the choice as a contract between leaders and the team, of which the OKR is one form and a list of projects is not.

Larson's capacity-first planning answers how much goes where and Build What Matters' vision-first planning answers what it is for; the two agree that shares come before items and conflict only where one is asked to do the other's job.
A planning cycle is shortened by removing what it should not be deciding: with the first two decisions settled once a year by named owners, only the choice of outcomes recurs each quarter.

role.contribution: Joins the two anchors at the point where they meet, which is the book's central integration.

additional_patterns.applies_to: three-decisions, envelope-and-allocation, outcomes-and-objectives, where-anchors-meet: the three decisions are named before the two patterns that carry them out, and both patterns come before the join between the sources, which compares what each pattern drew on.

flow.rationale: The reader first meets a planning process that failed, then the three decisions it was made of, then how the first two are made and held and how the third is made and recorded. Only then are the two anchor sources set against each other, because the comparison needs both patterns on the page; put earlier it would compare two books the reader had not yet seen at work. The failures and the worked example follow the full model so that the example can be read against one idea, separate decisions joined by objectives, and the AI section comes after the example because it changes the example's cadence.

hook.content: In 2026 Corvane's quarterly planning took nine of the quarter's thirteen weeks, and three weeks into the quarter it had planned, three teams found they were building the same integration.

bridge.from_reader_world: Most readers have sat in planning in which a question about one team's goals reopens the headcount, and a headcount change reopens everyone's goals.
bridge.to_topic: Planning of that kind is one negotiation where there should be three decisions; the question is how planning the capacity and planning the outcomes fit into one process.

thesis_statement.text: Capacity planning and outcome planning fit into one process as successive decisions: the financial plan fixes how much can be spent, allocation assigns capacity to areas and holds it steady, each area then chooses from the vision-led roadmap the outcomes its capacity will pursue, and team objectives record that choice as a contract between leaders and teams.

Learn the three decisions planning is made of and why they are made in order.
Learn how the financial plan is fixed and the allocation held.
Learn how outcomes are chosen from the roadmap and written as team objectives.
See how the book's two anchor sources fit together and where they would conflict.
Follow Corvane's plan run again as three decisions in three weeks.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2026 Corvane spent nine of a quarter's thirteen weeks planning the next quarter, and the plan still had three teams building the same integration.

evidence.what: Corvane, the fictional company this book follows. 2026, about 500 people, about thirty teams in four product groups. Planning the next quarter took nine of thirteen weeks; three weeks into the planned quarter three teams found they were building the same integration.
evidence.shows: A long planning process that still failed at the one thing a plan is for, making many teams' work consistent in advance.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Capacity planning and outcome planning fit into one process as three successive decisions with different owners, joined by team objectives, and the chapter takes them in that order.

transition_in.carries_over: Planning that takes most of a quarter and does not align the work; from the previous chapter, a decision right as a named decider, required advice and a record.
transition_in.introduces: Planning as the largest recurring set of decisions, how its rights are divided, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: The Nine-Week Plan
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane's planning was one negotiation in which headcount, features and team goals were settled together, group by group, and it cost both time and the consistency a plan exists to give.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case of tangled planning that the chapter explains and later runs again.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's short account of the nine weeks.
transition_in.introduces: How the planning ran and what it produced.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each director brought one document that held headcount requests, features and team goals together, and met the executives in turn, so that a change in one group's headcount reopened the documents of the others.

evidence.what: Corvane 2026, about 500 people, 260 in product and tech, about thirty teams in four product groups each under a director. Planning for the third quarter began in the fourth week of the second quarter and ended in its last week. The executives in the meetings: Ines Okafor (CEO), Tomas Rell (CTO), Priya Nambiar (CPO), Dario Vance (VP Engineering) and the head of finance. Each group was met separately, in several rounds.
evidence.shows: Budget, headcount, roadmap and goals were one subject, negotiated with every director, with no decision that stayed made.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The plan that came out hid a duplicate and gave up a share nobody was holding: three teams in three groups planned a connector to the same wholesaler, and two groups spent their operation share on features.

evidence.what: The Parts team, Stock Integrations and Technician App, in three different product groups, each had a connector to the same parts wholesaler's ordering system in its plan, each for a goal of its own group; they found out in the third week of the quarter, when two of them asked the wholesaler for a test account. Two of the four groups spent the operation share (the 25 percent of capacity the roadmap keeps for work on how the product is built and run) on features, as the engineering strategy's review found (chapter 13).
evidence.shows: Each group's plan was settled in its own meetings, so nobody read the plans together, and a share stated on the roadmap was traded away because no decision held it.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: One negotiation, group by group.
transition_in.introduces: What the plan it produced contained and what it had given up.

sections.heading: Three Decisions, Not One
sections.controlling_idea: Planning is made of three decisions that differ in question, information, decider and rate of change, and they work when made in order and separately.

advances_thesis.how: States Larson's three discussions as the model, and answers the opposing view of project-based planning.

flow.rationale: The source's model comes first, then the properties that make the three decisions different, then their order as a figure, and only then the opposing view, which can be judged once the reader has the three decisions to hold it against.

transition_in.carries_over: A negotiation in which nothing stayed decided.
transition_in.introduces: The decisions that negotiation was made of, according to Larson.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In The Engineering Executive's Primer, Larson describes planning as three things done in three separate discussions: the financial plan, the allocation of engineering's capacity, and the roadmap.

evidence.what: Larson, Primer, planning chapter: a planning process is effective to the extent that it sets the company's resource allocation across functions in an annual financial plan, refreshes engineering's functional portfolio allocation between functional and business priorities, and establishes with Product and Sales a high-level roadmap for a quarter or a half; the three phases are held in that order. The author's record of the chapter is the 'Planning' record in grounded-engineering-executive. Capacity is defined here as the working time of people in teams.
evidence.shows: The anchor source's model, named with its concept, on which the rest of the chapter builds.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), planning chapter; author's Kindle notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three decisions differ in the question each answers, in who holds the information, in who decides and in how often the answer should change.

evidence.what: Three rows (financial plan, allocation, choice of outcomes) by four columns: the question; who has the information; who decides; how often it should change (yearly; yearly and narrowly in between; every quarter). The lead-in says that team objectives, defined later in the chapter, record the third decision. The assignment of deciders follows the thesis's how-and-why and is the author's reading of Larson.
evidence.shows: Three decisions with three different owners and three different rates of change cannot be made well in one meeting by one group.

transition_in.carries_over: Larson's three discussions.
transition_in.introduces: What makes them three different decisions.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Made in order, each decision fixes what the next one works within, and team objectives record the last.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart, left to right: the financial plan (CEO with finance and the executive team; yearly) → the allocation (product and engineering executives; yearly, held) → the choice of outcomes (each area's leaders and teams; quarterly), with the vision-led roadmap entering at the third decision and team objectives coming out of it; an edge back from measured results to the roadmap.
evidence.shows: The order, who decides each step and where the roadmap enters.

transition_in.carries_over: Three different decisions.
transition_in.introduces: The order in which they are made and what each hands to the next.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Project-based planning, which funds and ranks projects each cycle, is right for a single large investment judged on its own and wrong as the unit of all planning, because ranking projects makes the three decisions at once, with the least information, and makes them again every cycle.

evidence.what: The opposing view's ground: a business case is a sound discipline for a discrete investment such as an acquisition or a new product line. Where it stops: a ranked project carries its own money, its own people and its own content, so the ranking decides budget, allocation and content together at the level where executives know least; and because every project competes again each cycle, nothing started is safe. Larson lists planning narrowly focused on project prioritization among the signs of planning that diminishes ownership, and prefers executives to prioritize outcomes.
evidence.shows: Grants the opposing view its ground and shows where it fails, which is the thesis's how-and-why.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), planning chapter; author's Kindle notes

transition_in.carries_over: Three decisions made separately and in order.
transition_in.introduces: The common alternative, in which the unit of decision is a funded project.

sections.heading: Pattern: Fix the Envelope, Then Hold the Allocation
sections.controlling_idea: The first two decisions are made once a year and then held: the financial plan as a fixed envelope, the allocation as whole teams and stated shares assigned to areas and changed only narrowly.

advances_thesis.how: Sets out the first two decisions as a pattern with a user and an outcome measure, and argues why the allocation is held.

flow.rationale: The envelope comes before the allocation that divides it; why the allocation is held comes after what it is; how it changes comes last, because a rule for change presupposes the reason for stability.

transition_in.carries_over: The three decisions in order.
transition_in.introduces: The first two as one pattern: what is fixed, and for how long.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The financial plan fixes, once a year, how much the organization can spend, and it is kept fixed so that teams work within it and do not work on moving it.

evidence.what: Larson, Primer: engineering's primary contribution to the financial plan is managing its expenses, which he segments into headcount, production operating costs and development costs; a durable plan focuses teams on executing within it, a flexible one on moving the constraint, for example by asking for more headcount; frequent adjustment makes execution impossible to grade.
evidence.shows: Why the envelope is decided first and then left alone.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), planning chapter; author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: "it's much easier to run an effective company with a stable financial plan."
evidence.shows: States the source's position in its own words.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), planning chapter; author's Kindle notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The allocation assigns capacity to areas in large units, whole teams to groups and a stated share to each kind of work, with a standing share for unproven ideas, and it does not assign people to projects.

evidence.what: Larson, Primer: functional portfolio allocation; 'The larger the granularity that you allocate, the more you empower your team to lead their teams'; new ideas are unscoped and unproven and should not be compared with proven work, so he suggests a long-running allocation for validating new projects and gives 10 percent of product engineering time as an example (his example, not a rule). The share by kind of work is the innovation, iteration and operation share of chapter 11.
evidence.shows: What the second decision contains and why its units are large.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), planning chapter; author's Kindle notes

transition_in.carries_over: A fixed envelope.
transition_in.introduces: How the envelope is divided among areas.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The allocation is held steady because a team can commit to an outcome that takes several quarters only if its people and its scope will still be there, and every rebalancing destroys part of what was started.

evidence.what: "Changing your allocation feels like progress, but each change is fairly disruptive, so there's a significant penalty to making frequent changes."
evidence.shows: Larson's reason for steady allocation.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), planning chapter; author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: Larson, An Elegant Puzzle: he is skeptical of reallocating individuals to answer shifts in priority, because teams take long to gel and have high fixed costs; he prefers moving scope between teams to moving people.
evidence.shows: The cost of a change falls on the team as a unit, which is why the unit of allocation is the team.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's Kindle notes

transition_in.carries_over: An allocation in large units.
transition_in.introduces: Why it is then left alone.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The allocation changes at a yearly review and by written proposal in between, and the changes follow the state each team is in and not the size of its request; its users are the directors and teams who plan against it, and it has worked when the changes made outside the review can be counted on one hand.

evidence.what: Larson's four team states in An Elegant Puzzle (falling behind, treading water, repaying debt, innovating), set out in chapter 5: people are added to a team that is falling behind, and the other states have other remedies. Larson, Primer: review the full set of engineering investments once a year or so. The use of the states as the basis for the yearly allocation review, the user and the outcome measure are the author's.
evidence.shows: Gives the narrow, intentional change a basis and the pattern its user and measure.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's Kindle notes

transition_in.carries_over: An allocation that is held.
transition_in.introduces: When and on what basis it does change.

sections.heading: Pattern: Choose Outcomes from the Roadmap, and Write Them as Team Objectives
sections.controlling_idea: The third decision takes the vision-led roadmap as its input: each area chooses the outcomes its allocated capacity will pursue, and a team objective records each choice as a contract.

advances_thesis.how: Shows where the roadmap of chapter 11 enters the process and defines the team objective as the contract that joins capacity to outcome.

flow.rationale: The choice comes first, then the objective that records it, then the best-known form of an objective, and last the test that separates an objective from a project list, which needs the definition before it.

transition_in.carries_over: Capacity fixed and assigned to areas.
transition_in.introduces: What that capacity is for, which is decided third and by other people.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The third decision does not write the roadmap: the roadmap exists before planning starts, and each area's leaders choose from it, in the open, the outcomes that the area's capacity will pursue in the coming quarter.

evidence.what: Larson, Primer, on agreeing the roadmap: done with Product and Design; the frequent mistake is to resolve it in a series of one-on-one discussions; emphasize the target outcome first at high confidence and the specific project second at lower confidence, and the team may change the project while it stays aligned with the outcome. The roadmap itself (outcomes in an order, three horizons) is chapter 11's, derived from the vision and strategy of chapter 10.
evidence.shows: Larson's third discussion and the roadmap of Build What Matters are the same step seen from two sides: he says how to hold it, the roadmap says what is on the table.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), planning chapter; author's Kindle notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team objective is an outcome a team answers for over a stated period, with a measure and a target, and it is a contract because each side commits something to the other.

evidence.what: Two columns, what leaders commit and what the team commits. Leaders: the problem and why it comes now; the measure of success; the capacity, held for the period; no new work added without something taken off. Team: the target it proposed for the measure; the solution, which it chooses; reporting gaps and risks as they appear; a result reviewed against the measure. The division follows Cagan and Jones, Empowered (leaders assign problems with context, teams propose key results), through the author's record team-objectives and chapter 12; reading it as a contract whose leaders' side includes the held capacity is the author's synthesis.
evidence.shows: The objective is where the allocation (capacity held) and the roadmap (outcome chosen) are written on one page.
evidence.source: Marty Cagan with Chris Jones, Empowered (2020), through grounded-product-management/team-objectives

transition_in.carries_over: Outcomes chosen for each area.
transition_in.introduces: The form in which the choice is recorded for each team.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The OKR, an objective with a few measurable key results, is the best-known form of a team objective and one form among several; what the form must keep is the outcome, the measure, the target and the owner.

evidence.what: From the author's sources: the grammar in the author's record writing-okrs, built on the workbook to Claire Hughes Johnson's Scaling People (three to five objectives per team, one to five key results each, each objective labeled committed or aspirational). Supplementing the author's sources, and marked so in the text: John Doerr's Measure What Matters (2018) and its site whatmatters.com, which credits the method to Andy Grove at Intel, says Doerr introduced it at Google in 1999 and calls key results 'measurable and verifiable'; Christina Wodtke, author of Radical Focus (2016), who in 'The Art of the OKR' (2014) recommends one set of OKRs per team. Both web pages were fetched and read on 2026-11-19.
evidence.shows: Credits OKR practice to its sources and separates what the author's bookshelf supports from what supplements it.
evidence.source: grounded-people-management-tools/writing-okrs; whatmatters.com; eleganthack.com

transition_in.carries_over: The team objective as a contract.
transition_in.introduces: Its best-known form, and where that form comes from.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A list of projects is not an objective, because a project can be delivered in full while nothing changes for a customer; the pattern's users are the teams and the leaders who review them, and it has worked when every objective is reviewed by its measure at the end of the period.

evidence.what: Two statements for one Corvane team: 'Ship the wholesaler connector by week 9' and 'Jobs that need a second visit for a missing part fall from 9 percent to 7 percent' (the ledger's driver: 14 percent at the end of 2024, 9 percent at the end of 2025, target 7). The first can be true while the second has not moved. The projects by which a team reaches its objective are the team's business (chapter 12).
evidence.shows: The test that separates an objective from a project list, on a ledger number.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: Objectives in a sound form.
transition_in.introduces: The commonest thing written in that form that is not an objective.

sections.heading: Where the Two Anchors Meet
sections.controlling_idea: Larson plans from capacity and Build What Matters from the vision; they answer different questions, agree that shares come before items, and would conflict in three places, each of which the book settles by keeping each to its own question.

advances_thesis.how: States the integration of the two anchor sources explicitly, with the points of conflict and the book's resolution, marked as the author's.

flow.rationale: Each source is stated fairly first, then the two are set side by side, then the places where they would collide, and the resolution comes last because it is a claim about the collisions.

transition_in.carries_over: Two patterns, the first drawn from Larson and the second from the vision-led roadmap and Empowered.
transition_in.introduces: The join between the two sources, stated outright.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two sources plan from opposite ends, Larson from money and people with the roadmap last, and Foster and Nerlikar from the customer's future with the roadmap as its consequence, and they agree on two things: a share is decided before any item, and outcomes come before projects.

evidence.what: Larson, Primer: financial plan, then allocation, then a high-level roadmap for a quarter or a half; outcomes first, projects second. Foster and Nerlikar, Build What Matters: the vision in the customer's terms, strategic milestones, the roadmap that connects near-term work to them, and a top-down allocation among innovation, iteration and operation made before items are ranked ('big decisions need to come before small ones').
evidence.shows: Each source stated in its own terms, and the common ground that makes a join possible.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), planning chapter; author's Kindle notes; Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020); author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: "This should be obvious, but big decisions need to come before small ones."
evidence.shows: Build What Matters states the principle Larson's sequence also follows.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020); author's Kindle notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Set side by side, the two answer different questions for different readers, and each goes wrong in a recognizable way when it is asked to answer the other's.

evidence.what: Rows: starts from; the question it answers; what it fixes; what it leaves open; written for; asked to do the other's job. Columns: Larson (capacity first), Build What Matters (vision first). Larson asked to choose content gives a ranked list of projects with headcount; Build What Matters asked to set capacity gives a roadmap in which every outcome arrives with a request for people.
evidence.shows: The two are complements with a defined failure when either is stretched over the other's question.

transition_in.carries_over: Opposite starting points and two shared rules.
transition_in.introduces: The two set side by side, row by row.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two would conflict in three places: when the roadmap needs more capacity than the allocation gives, when each source's share is decided in a different room, and when the roadmap's reassessment meets the plan's stability; the book settles each by a rule.

evidence.what: Three rows: where they would conflict; what each source would do; the book's rule. (1) The roadmap needs more than the allocation gives: the allocation holds for the year, the order and timing of outcomes move, and the shortfall goes to the yearly review. (2) Two shares cut the same capacity: Larson's functional portfolio allocation, set by the engineering executive, and the operation share of Build What Matters, set in product planning; the book makes it one decision, taken jointly by the product and engineering executives, with engineering's own priorities inside the operation share (chapter 13's allocation policy). (3) Rhythm: Build What Matters reassesses roadmap and vision at each third or quarter of the horizon, Larson holds plan and allocation steady; a reassessment changes outcomes and their order and reaches the allocation only at its review.
evidence.shows: Makes the points of conflict explicit, as the blocker criterion requires, and gives the rule for each.

transition_in.carries_over: Complementary questions.
transition_in.introduces: The places where the two would nonetheless pull against each other.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The book's resolution, which is the author's and which neither source states, is that Larson answers how much goes where, Build What Matters answers what it is for, team objectives join the two, and they conflict only when one is asked to do the other's job.

evidence.what: Neither book addresses the other's subject at length: Larson's roadmap phase is a few pages on how to hold the discussion, and Build What Matters says little about budgets or headcount. The join through team objectives draws on a third source, Empowered. The resolution is therefore marked as the author's synthesis.
evidence.shows: States the thesis's central integration and its status as the author's.

transition_in.carries_over: Three conflicts, each settled by keeping a source to its own question.
transition_in.introduces: The general rule behind the three.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: The Consensus Stall and the Output Scoreboard
sections.controlling_idea: Planning fails in two of the book's named ways: as a Consensus Stall when its decisions have no owners, and as an Output Scoreboard when its objectives are lists of projects reviewed by delivery.

advances_thesis.how: Lets the reader recognize the two failures the patterns prevent, using the book's failure-pattern names.

transition_in.carries_over: The process as it should run.
transition_in.introduces: The two ways it most often fails.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each of the two failure patterns has a form specific to planning, a sign by which to recognize it and a missing piece that explains it.

evidence.what: Two rows. The Consensus Stall (a decision with no named decider, finished only when everyone with a stake agrees): in planning, budget, headcount, roadmap and goals negotiated together; signs: planning meetings end by scheduling another, a settled headcount is reopened by a roadmap question; missing: an owner and a record for each of the three decisions. The Output Scoreboard (an organization that counts what was produced and does not ask what changed for a customer): in planning, objectives that are projects with dates, reviewed by the share delivered; signs: the review reports what shipped; missing: a measure and a target in each objective, and a review by outcome.
evidence.shows: Ties the chapter's two patterns to the two failures they answer.
evidence.source: where-product-and-tech-organizations-go-wrong (the failure-patterns page)

sections.heading: Worked Example: The Nine-Week Plan as Three Decisions
sections.controlling_idea: Run again as three decisions with owners, Corvane's planning took three weeks, and the duplicate that nine weeks had hidden was found in an afternoon.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the separation and the join by objectives to the case of the opening, and shows what was removed from the quarterly cycle.

flow.rationale: The three weeks are shown first as they ran, then what they show about the separation, then the duplicate as the test of the join by objectives, then the costs, which can be weighed only after the result.

transition_in.carries_over: Two patterns, the join between the sources and two failures.
transition_in.introduces: All of it applied to the planning of the opening scene.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the end of 2026 Corvane planned the first quarter of 2027 as three decisions, each with one question, an owner, required advice, a record and a week.

evidence.what: Three rows (illustrative figures). Week 1, the financial plan for 2027: decided by Ines Okafor with the head of finance, after advice from Tomas Rell, Priya Nambiar and Dario Vance; product and tech grows from 260 to 284 people during 2027, with a month for each hire and budgets for production and development costs; fixed for the year. Week 2, the allocation: decided together by Priya Nambiar and Tomas Rell, as Corvane's 2025 page of executive decision rights has it, after written advice from Dario Vance and the four directors; the thirty teams stay in their groups, the twenty-four hires go to newer teams too small to staff their own on-call rotation and none to the platform team, the shares stay at 40, 35 and 25 with the operation share going first to migrations; held for 2027, changed only by a written proposal to both. Week 3, the choice of outcomes: each group's director with its product managers chooses at most three outcomes from the roadmap, in the order the CPO has set; each team proposes its targets and writes one or two objectives; all objectives are published in one place and read together in one open session.
evidence.shows: The same subjects as the nine weeks, divided so that each meeting had one question and one decider.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three weeks were short because the quarterly cycle no longer decided the budget or the allocation: two of the three decisions were made once for the year and were not reopened by the third.

evidence.what: In the nine weeks every director's meeting could reopen headcount; in the three weeks a director who wanted more people had a written proposal to two named executives and no place for it in week 3. In the remaining quarters of 2027 only the third decision recurs.
evidence.shows: Shortening came from removing what the quarterly cycle should not be deciding, the third can-do of the chapter.

transition_in.carries_over: Three weeks, three decisions.
transition_in.introduces: Why three weeks were enough.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The duplicate was found in the open session of the third week, because three teams' objectives, published side by side, each named the same wholesaler connector as work toward a target of its own.

evidence.what: Parts, Stock Integrations and Technician App each listed the connector to the parts wholesaler under its objective. The three directors agreed in the session that Stock Integrations builds it once and the other two teams use it; the dependency was written into the two teams' objectives. The separation of decisions did not find the duplicate by itself; publishing the objectives together and reading them in one session did.
evidence.shows: The join by objectives, and not the separation alone, is what made the plans of many teams consistent.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: Time saved by separating the decisions.
transition_in.introduces: What the written objectives added: the duplicate became visible.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The change had costs and proves little yet: directors lost a quarterly lever, a wrong allocation now lasts longer, and one planning cycle is not a result.

evidence.what: Directors can no longer trade headcount each quarter; a misjudged allocation stays until a written proposal or the yearly review corrects it; the first week rested on a financial plan finance had prepared through the autumn, so three weeks is the length of the deciding and not of the preparation; no outcome of the first quarter of 2027 is claimed.
evidence.shows: States the limits of the illustration honestly.

transition_in.introduces: What they cost and what they do not show.

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: If agents shorten the learning cycle, the third decision speeds up and the first two do not, and the financial plan gains a cost that trades against headcount.

advances_thesis.how: Tests the separation of the three decisions against a shorter learning cycle, with labeled claims.

transition_in.carries_over: A quarterly third decision, set by Corvane's learning cycle of about a quarter.
transition_in.introduces: What happens to the cadence if that cycle shortens.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A shorter learning cycle shortens the cadence of the third decision only, because the financial plan and the allocation are paced by the fiscal year, by hiring and by how long a team takes to learn its area, none of which is building time.

evidence.what: Opens with the label scheme. Emerging (the author's observation, as in chapter 11, not a measured result): coding agents shorten the building of a first version, so the learning cycle (the time from deciding to try a solution to knowing whether it moved the outcome) may shorten, by less than the building does. Speculative: objectives would then be chosen and reviewed by cycle and not by calendar quarter, while the first two decisions stay yearly; an organization whose three decisions are tangled cannot speed up the third without reopening the other two. Confirmed where organizations report objective cycles shorter than a quarter under an unchanged yearly budget and allocation.
evidence.shows: The separation matters more, not less, when one of the three decisions speeds up.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Agent spending enters the financial plan as a development cost that grows with use and can be traded against headcount, which makes the first decision harder and counting capacity in people less complete.

evidence.what: Speculative: of Larson's three cost segments, agent usage falls under development costs and, unlike a tool license, grows with the work done; the first decision then weighs it against headcount, and an allocation counted in people leaves part of capacity out. Corvane's 2028 plan asks whether to hire engineers at all (the Hiring Question). Confirmed where financial plans state agent spending and headcount as one traded line. The full argument is chapter 41.
evidence.shows: Marks what the chapter's model assumed (capacity is people) and hands the argument to the chapter that owns it.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.introduces: A change inside the first.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Planning aligns many teams when it is three decisions with three owners and three rates of change, and the team objective is the one page on which the capacity held and the outcome chosen meet; the length of a planning cycle measures how many of the three it is deciding at once.
conclusion.so_what: A leader stops ranking projects, keeps allocation stable across cycles, and reviews objectives by outcome.

callback.to: Corvane's nine-week plan and the three teams building the same integration.
callback.how: The reader can now say what the nine weeks were deciding and why they could not find the duplicate, and what three weeks with owners and published objectives did differently.

takeaway.content: List what your last planning cycle decided, sort each item under the financial plan, the allocation or the choice of outcomes, name an owner for each of the three, and rewrite one team's project list as an objective.
